This is an appeal U/Sec. 29 of the Protection Protection of Woman from Domestic Violence Act,
2005 (hereinafter referred to as 'DV Act') against the order dated 12.10.2023 (hereinafter referred to as 'impugned order') passed by Ld. Trial Court in CT Case No. 2684/2020 titled as "Shikha Kumar Vs. Harjeet Singh Kumar" whereby Ld. Trial Court has passed interim order and appellant no. 1 (husband) herein was directed to pay interim maintenance of Rs. 50,000/- to the complainant from the date of filing of petition i.e. 18.03.2020 till the disposal of the case.

sentences.text: I have heard arguments addressed by respective Ld. Counsels of the parties and carefully perused the record including the record of Ld. Trial Court.
9. The phenomenon of domestic violence is widely prevalent but has remained largely invisible in the public domain.
Where a woman is subjected to cruelty by her husband or her relatives.
The civil law does not however address this phenomenon in its entirety.

It was therefore, proposed to enact a law keeping in view of the rights guaranteed under Article 14, 15 & 21 of the Constitution to provide for a remedy under the civil law which is intended to protect the woman from being victims of domestic violence and to prevalent the occurrence of the domestic violence in the society.

Keeping these objects and reasons in mind to provide for more effective protection of the rights of the woman guaranteed under Constitution who are victims of violence of any kind occurring within the family and for matter connected therewith or incidental thereto, the Bill was presented and the Protection of Woman From Domestic Violence Act, 2005 was passed by the Parliament.

entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: Thus, it cannot be lost sight of, that the Act has been passed keeping in view the provision under the Constitution and to provide a remedy under the civil law which is intended to protect the woman from domestic violence in the society.

We may also see that where an alternative constructions are possible, the court must give effect to that which will be responsible for the smooth working of the CA No. 262/2024 Harjeet Singh Kumar Vs. Shikha Kumar Page no. 7 of 14 system for which the statute has been enacted rather than the one which would put hindrances in its way.

sentences.text: If the choice is between two interpretations, the narrower of which would fail to achieve the manifest purpose of the legislation, we should avoid a construction which would reduce the legislation to futility.

10. The Act inter-alia provides for more effective protection or the right of woman guaranteed under the constitution who are victims of the domestic violence of any kind occurring within the shared household.
According to the Act, any harm, injury to health, safety, life, limb or well being or any other act or threatening or coercion etc. by any adult member of the family, constitutes domestic violence.
Further, the act also contemplates that any woman who is or has been in a domestic relationship, if she is subjected to any domestic violence can file a complaint u/sec. 12 of the PWDV Act.

This Act also covers those woman who are or have been in relationship with the abuser where both parties have live together in a shared household and a relative by consanguinity, marriage or through a relationship in the nature of marriage or adoption.
In addition, the relationship with the family members living together as a joint family are also included.

Even those women are sisters,
widows, mothers or single woman or living with the abuses, are entitled to legal protection.

sentences.text: 4 11. Section 22 of PWDV Act, 2005, gives the relief of compensation the aggrieved person.
This section of the Act allows Magistrates to order compensation and damages for injuries caused by domestic violence.
This includes mental torture and emotional distress.

However, the considerations deliberating for determination of compensation in domestic violence cases is required to be considered by the Court as the aggrieved person which is the complainant in the present matter, has been a victim of domestic violence.
The central question is whether compensation should be based on the severity of violence or the perpetrator's financial capacity.
The court aims to address whether compensation should align with the degree of violence suffered or the financial status of the perpetrator.
The DV Act aims to enhance the protection of women's rights guaranteed under the Constitution.

It covers various forms of abuse, including physical, sexual,
verbal, emotional, and economic abuse.

Section 3 of the Act defines domestic violence,
encompassing acts or conduct that harm or endanger the victim's health, safety, or well-being.

The Domestic Violence Act explicitly states that domestic violence includes actions aimed at coercing the aggrieved person or her relatives to meet unlawful dowry demands or surrender property or valuable security.
This provision emphasizes the Act's broader scope, encompassing not only physical harm but also financial coercion and manipulation.

The Act defines an "aggrieved person"
as any woman who is currently or has been in a domestic relationship with the respondent.

This definition underscores the Act's gender-specific focus on protecting women who have CA No.
262/2024 Harjeet Singh Kumar Vs. Shikha Kumar Page no. 9 of 14 experienced domestic violence.

sentences.text: It recognizes the complexity of domestic relationships and ensures legal recourse for those subjected to abuse within such relationships.
By defining domestic violence comprehensively and specifying the aggrieved person's identity, the Domestic Violence Act provides a robust framework for legal interpretation and enforcement.
Therefore, it is incumbent upon the Court to use these definitions to evaluate cases and determine appropriate remedies and compensation for victims.
Therefore, the relief of compensation Under Section 22 of the Domestic Violence Act empowers Magistrates to order compensation and damages for injuries caused by acts of domestic violence.

This provision allows for additional relief beyond other remedies available under the Act which are discretionary to the Court but at the same time, should be awarded by taking into consideration facts and circumstances of each case.
Compensation encompasses not only physical injuries but also mental torture and emotional distress inflicted upon the aggrieved person.
It acknowledges the holistic impact of domestic violence on victims' well-being and seeks to address both visible and invisible forms of harm.
Section 12 of the Domestic Violence Act grants the aggrieved person or their representative the right to seek various reliefs under the Act, including compensation.

Importantly,
it preserves the aggrieved person's right to pursue compensation through civil suits independently of the Act, however at the same time, it does not take away the right of the complainant or the aggrieved person to seek compensation from the court by substantiating the acts of domestic violence which may be CA No. 262/2024 Harjeet Singh Kumar Vs. Shikha Kumar Page no. 10 of 14 physical, mental, economical etc.

sentences.text: Ld. Counsel for the appellant/ husband has argued that while the standard of living might apply to maintenance cases under Section 20, the compensation awarded in this instance was based on the appellant's income.

At the same time, Section 20 of the Domestic Violence Act allows magistrates to order monetary relief to meet expenses and losses suffered by the aggrieved person and any children, aligning with their accustomed standard of living.
The magistrate can decide on lump sum payments or monthly maintenance based on the case's nature and circumstances.

Further the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in the case of Chaturbhuj vs. Sita Bai AIR 2008 Supreme Court 530,
emphasized preventing destitution in maintenance proceedings rather than punishing neglectful spouses.

As courts navigate the complexities of domestic violence cases, it is incumbent upon the Court to consider both the specific injuries suffered by victims and the broader context of financial implications for all parties involved.
The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 is an Act of the Parliament of India enacted to protect women from domestic violence.

Further, the plea of appellant/ husband that he has responsibility of his ailing mother and some loans amounts,
cannot absolve him from the responsibility of his legal wedded wife and children and only an attempt has been made by appellant/ husband in this regard just to avoid his responsibility towards his wife and children.

Further, perusal of the record also shows huge transactions in the bank accounts of appellant/ husband, which cannot be lost sight off, although he has tried to downplay the said income shown in his bank accounts by taking the grounds that he has to pay certain loan amounts taken from different institutions including family and friends and is under heavy debt.
In these circumstances it would be suffice to hold that complainant has a legal right to get the relief.
No prudent man/ husband is expected to take such pleas and showing his helplessness in paying the interim maintenance to his wife.

Hence, merely because the appellant/ husband may be required to pay loan amounts and responsibility of his ailing mother and debts, will not diminish his responsibility to maintain his wife or children.

sentences.text: The observation of Ld. Trial Court to give interim maintenance of Rs.50,000/- per month to complainant/ respondent, cannot be considered as non-judicious and irrational and the Ld. Trial Court has given reasons for the same in 'para 9, 10 & 11' of the impugned order and has also taken into consideration the fact that complainant/ respondent is also earning.

The complainant in the present matter, has substantiated her allegations against the appellants by relying upon the documents and has also stated that it was the respondents who had committed the acts of domestic violence upon the complainant which led to her filing of the complaint u/sec. 12 of the Domestic Violence Act.

Therefore, I am of the considered opinion that appellant/ husband Harjeet Singh Kumar is capable of paying the interim maintenance to complainant/ respondent Shikha Kumar, as awarded by Ld. Trial Court vide impugned order dated 12.10.2023.
16.
In view of the aforesaid appreciation, Ld. Trial Court has carefully dealt with the contentions raised on behalf of both the parties and I find no infirmity in the impugned order.
Hence, I conclude that Ld. Trial Court had passed the impugned order legally and correctly.
It was not perverse in nature and needs no interference.
Present Appeal, therefore stands dismissed.
Ordered accordingly.
